ann.l: Large polygonal tumor cells with abundant clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm and a round central nucleus create the classic 'fried-egg' appearance. Glycogen dissolves during routine slide preparation, leaving the distinctive pale halo.

Nests of tumor cells are separated by thin fibrovascular septa containing prominent infiltrates of small, dark, mature lymphocytes. This T-cell-rich immune response is a signature histological feature of testicular seminoma.

Neighboring cells maintain crisp, well-defined cytoplasmic membranes that produce a sharp polygonal mosaic. This orderly architecture directly contrasts with the messy, overlapping, syncytial borders of embryonal carcinoma.

Nuclei throughout the tumor nests share a remarkably uniform size, round contour, vesicular chromatin, and prominent central nucleoli, reflecting homogeneous germ-cell differentiation rather than the extreme pleomorphism of embryonal carcinoma.

findings: Fried-egg cells: large polygonal tumor cells with a central round nucleus, a prominent nucleolus and clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm bounded by a sharp cell membrane fill most of the field.
Lymphocytes: clusters of small, dark, round lymphocytes lie between the tumor nests, especially at the right and left edges; this infiltrate along the thin septa is a hallmark of seminoma.

Distinct cell borders: the membranes of neighboring tumor cells stay crisp, giving each cell a well-defined polygonal outline in the central nests, unlike the overlapping, indistinct borders of embryonal carcinoma.
Uniform nuclei: the nuclei are all similar in size, round and vesicular with coarse chromatin, which contrasts with the pleomorphic, overlapping nuclei of embryonal carcinoma.
